lead.t: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch and perinatal stress are prevalent in meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS)

snip.t: Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch and perinatal stress are prevalent in meconium aspiration syndrome (MAS)
Spontaneous/Traumatic breach → Air entry → Loss of negative intrapleural pressure → Lung recoil → Collapse → Decreased ventilation‑perfusion matching → Hypoxaemia

Pulmonary vasculature (bronchial circulation) – supplies airway walls; can become engorged in chronic inflammation.: Vascular engorgement contributes to airway wall thickening and may worsen ventilation‑perfusion mismatch in advanced disease.
Ventilation‑perfusion mismatch → chronic hypoxaemia, secondary polycythaemia, CO₂ retention

Ventilation‑perfusion (V/Q) matching – alveolar ventilation matched to pulmonary perfusion: Dilated, mucus‑filled bronchi cause regional hypoventilation, producing low V/Q units, hypoxaemia and dyspnoea that worsen with disease progression.

Respiratory mechanics – compliance, airway resistance, ventilation‑perfusion (V/Q) matching.: Obstructive tumours raise airway resistance → dyspnoea, atelectasis, V/Q mismatch → hypoxaemia; these physiologic changes explain the clinical picture of breathlessness and cough.
Explain ventilation, perfusion, diffusion and gas exchange.

es.q: Distinguish the types of ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) mismatch and provide clinical examples for each.
es.m:
- **Low V/Q mismatch**: Occurs when perfusion exceeds ventilation; clinical examples include pneumonia, asthma, COPD exacerbations, or pulmonary oedema.
- **High V/Q mismatch**: Occurs when ventilation exceeds perfusion; a classic clinical example is pulmonary embolism.
- **Shunt**: Blood passes through unventilated alveoli; examples include severe consolidation and atelectasis, where supplemental oxygen may have limited effect.
- **Diffusion impairment**: Results from a thickened or damaged alveolar-capillary membrane; a classic example is interstitial lung disease.
